seriesTitle: The Lantern Mender of Pell Street
title: Below the Wick
blurb: Ada is bound by a charter and handed the Provost's own dimming lantern. Some mends cost more than a memory.

blocks.text: Boots on Pell Street at first bell. Four pairs, in step.
Ada lifted her cheek off the ledger. She had fallen asleep at the bench again.
The boots stopped at her door. A hiss. The smell of hot wax. Something pressed hard into the wood.
Then a man's voice, clipped, pitched for the whole street. "By order under the charter, the outsider styling herself Mender will present herself to the Provost by third bell, or be escorted."
The boots went away.

Ada opened the door. A red seal the size of a saucer sat on the panel at head height, still soft, stamped with a lantern inside a ring. Someone was already on the step, basket on her arm, oilskin dark with drizzle.
"Oh, petal," Hester whispered. "What have you done?"
"Three lanterns," said Ada. "That's all I've done."
"That's plenty, love." Hester came in out of the wet and set the basket on the bench, the way she had every morning. Currant buns. Butter in a twist of paper. She did not hum.
Ada noticed, the way you notice a building go quiet when the power drops. You don't hear the hum until it stops.
"You're quiet."

"Up all night, my duck. Wind had half the lamps out down the bottom end, and me up and down the ladder like a sparrow." Hester buttered a bun with her gloves on and pushed it across. "Eat. Nobody goes to Harrow on an empty stomach. She'll have you for the second course."
"What's she like?"

Hester thought about it. "Cold room. Cold manner. Never says your name; she'll say what you are." She brushed crumbs off the bench with the side of her glove. "Fair, mind. Fair as a ruler, and about as cuddly. Say yes to whatever she puts in front of you, love. Saves time."

The Provost's hall stood on the square, across from the clock tower, and it was colder inside than out. Stone floor. High windows. A fireplace big enough to stand in, with nothing in it but swept brick. Every footstep came back twice.
Emrys was already there, at a small table to one side, the Register open and his pen ready. He looked up when Ada came in, and then down at the page, fast.

Provost Rosalind Harrow sat at the long table under the windows. Grey hair cut short as a brush. A dark coat buttoned to the chin. And on her hands, black gloves, fine and close, the kind you could write a letter in.
Ada looked at the gloves, and thought of a dark hand at the torn edge of a memory, fingers closing. She made herself look up.

"Mender," said Harrow. Not a greeting. A label. "The Registrar has reported an irregularity. An outsider. No lantern, no line. Practising a chartered craft on Pell Street. Three mends in four nights. Is that accurate?"
Ada glanced at Emrys. He had gone the colour of his paper.
"It's accurate."

"Then you will take the Oath." Harrow unrolled a sheet of heavy paper and read it without looking down, the way people read things they have said at funerals. "Under the charter of Morrow Quay. The Mender sees what the lanterns keep. The Mender may never speak a seen secret without the owner's leave. A Mender who breaks this Oath is exiled into the fog. And the first time she breaks it, her craft goes back to nothing. Below the wick." She laid the paper flat. "So noted."
Below the wick. Ada thought of the pale gold word that had been hers for four nights, and of it going out like a tripped breaker. Not Wick. Nothing.
"I already keep them," she said. "Secrets. Nobody had to tell me to."
"Then signing will cost you nothing."
"And if someone's in danger? If I see something that's going to hurt somebody?"
"Then you will find another way to say so, one that is not the secret." Harrow turned the paper round to face her. "The charter does not care how clever you are, Mender. It cares that you are bound."
"I've had bosses," said Ada. "Twelve years of them. I've never had a charter."
"You have one now."
"And if I don't sign?"
Harrow folded her gloved hands on the table. "The fog road is closed to walking out," she said. "It has never been closed to walking in."
Across the hall, Emrys's pen stopped scratching.

Ada stood there long enough to hear her own breath come back off the stone. Then she picked up the pen. It was heavy, a proper steel nib, and it caught on the paper the way a bad cable catches in a conduit. Ada Brannock. She did not make the signature look nice.
"Registrar," said Harrow. "Enter the Mender's Oath."
"There's no line for her, Provost."
A pause. Ada was beginning to learn that Harrow paused before giving anything away. "Then the margin."
So Ada signed in the margin of the Register for the second time in three days, with Emrys holding the book flat and not looking at her.

"One further matter." Harrow rose and crossed to the wall. Set into the stone was a cabinet with a glass front, and across its door ran a strip of red wax with the same lantern-in-a-ring. Behind the glass a lantern burned. Tall, plain, iron-framed. Its flame was small and bluish, like a gas ring turned right down. "The Provost's lantern is kept sealed in this hall, under the charter. It is dimming. You will mend it. Tonight. Here."
In the grey daylight the readout was barely there over the cabinet, a word too pale to read.
"No," said Ada.
Harrow turned. "I beg your pardon."
"You sealed my door at first bell and read me out in front of the whole street. I mend for people who ask."
"I am not asking."
"No," said Ada. "I'd noticed."
The longest pause yet. "Ninth bell, Mender. Registrar, see her out."
Gulls on the square. Wind off the water, cutting across the cobbles. Above them the clock face hung dark, its hands still.
Emrys came down the hall steps two at a time and then stopped, one step above her, so that for once they were eye to eye.
"I filed it," he said. "The irregularity. Four days ago. Before."
"Before you liked me?"
"Before I knew what you were for." He took his spectacles off, and looked at her properly. "You can refuse tonight."
"She just told me I can't."

"She told you she would prefer you didn't. That's different." He lowered his voice, though there was nobody near but gulls. "Her order isn't in the Register until I enter it. I could be slow. Misplace a page. For the record, I have never misplaced a page in my life, but I'm told it's easily done."
"And when she finds out?"
He looked back up at the hall door. When he spoke again it was very quiet.
"The Register serves at the Provost's pleasure. She can close it with one sentence."

Ada thought of the desk drawer at the top of his stair. One folded sheet. Eleven lines, and a twelfth that had gone grey while they watched. If the office shut, nobody in Morrow Quay would be watching that book at all.
"Then don't be slow," she said.

"Somebody has to keep your book open. I'll go." She tucked her hands into her armpits against the wind. "Test before you touch. I'll look at the thing first. If it's above me, I'll walk away and she can seal what she likes."
Emrys put his spectacles back on.
"I'll be on these steps," he said.
"It'll be freezing."
"I'm aware of the temperature. I'll be on the steps."
Ninth bell. Deep and slow, from across the water.
The hall at night was one lamp on the long table and a great deal of dark. Harrow stood by the cabinet. She was alone.
"No Registrar inside," she said, before Ada could ask. "No record."
Through the high window Ada could make out a thin shape on the steps, stamping its feet.
She went to the cabinet and did what she always did first. She looked.
In lamplight the readout came up clear over the sealed glass. WICK. Pale gold. Steady.
At or below her tier. She could touch it.
"Break the seal," Ada said. "Then stand back. Hands behind you."
Harrow put a gloved thumb to the wax. It cracked like a knuckle. She lifted the lantern out, set it on the long table, and did not move away.
"Further back. Hands behind you, please."
A pause. "So noted." Harrow stepped back and put her gloved hands behind her, like a woman inspecting a parade.

Ada bent to the lantern. A line of light ran up from the base, fine as a hair, and split into three near the top, like frost on a window. The glass was cold. Not warm the way the others had been. Cold as a pane in winter.
"How long's it been shut in there?"
"Ten years."
"Glass doesn't like cold and dark," said Ada. "Any more than people do."
Harrow said nothing.
Ada laid her fingers on either side of the crack, and the bar came up.

It came up slowly. Heavier than anything she had done. It was like pulling cable through a conduit that was already full, every inch a fight, and the ache started in her fingertips and climbed to her wrists and settled there.
"One," she said, out loud. She didn't mean to. "Two. Three."
The glass clicked under her hands. Warmer, now. The bar crept.
"Fourteen. Fifteen."
She heard Harrow shift behind her. She didn't look round.
"Thirty-one. Thirty-two."
And then the hall went away.
Lamplight. A desk.
Rain on a high window, hard.
A clock, ticking. Slow and heavy, somewhere very close. Ada had never heard the town clock tick.
A hand in a black glove, holding a pen.
Pieces. The page came in pieces, like a letter someone had torn up and was trying to read back.
*Order under the charter.*
*...the lower sluice...*
*...at once.*
The word *sluice* again, underlined.
A signature, quick and hard. *R. Harrow.*

The eyes Ada was seeing through turned to the window. Down the hill lay the canal quarter, and all along the lower quay, where there should have been a line of lamps on their iron posts, there was nothing. Dark, all the way along.
Ada knew that dark. She had stood in it, up to the knees, through someone else's eyes.
Back to the page. Lower down, smaller, the black glove wrote one more line.
*Lower-quay lamps unlit at ninth bell. Whose watch?*
The gloved fingers closed round the pen. They did not write any more.
A voice, younger but already clipped. "Not tonight."
Then the pieces scattered, and the ticking went with them.
"Forty-eight," said Ada, in the cold hall, with her eyes open. "Forty-nine."
The bar filled.
Over the lantern the pale gold word WICK thinned out, the way it did in daylight, and was gone. In its place, brighter, a new word came up.
GLASS.
"Glass," said Ada.
"What?"
"Nothing."
The flame inside rose, cleared and stood up white-gold, and the hairline crack was not there any more.

Ada straightened up. Her hands hurt. She flexed them, slowly, and told herself what she had told herself every working day for twelve years. Test before you touch. Somebody had said that to her first. A man with a flask of tea and a tape measure clipped to his belt, in her first week, in the back of a van that smelled of flux. She could see his hands. His thumbnail, split. She reached for his name.
Nothing there. Not even the first letter.
Four, she thought. Write it down. Rule two.
She looked back at the lantern, because she could not look at the hole where the name had been.
The readout had not faded yet. Under GLASS, smaller, sat a line she had never seen before.
Secrets held: 2.
Two. She had seen an order and a question. One secret, or two? Or one she hadn't seen at all?

Behind her, Harrow had brought her hands round from her back. She took her coat from the chair and pulled it on, buttoning it to the chin with black-gloved fingers, and she did not look at the lantern once.
"Whatever you saw, Mender," said Provost Harrow, "you saw nothing. Or you walk into the fog."
